We’re living through the most transformational moment of our careers, and I'm here to expose it. I have a team that can cover it all.

amplemarket-growth-and-elite-customers-p.headline: Amplemarket Growth \u0026 Elite Customers - Pricing Credits \u0026 Duo Copilot
amplemarket-growth-and-elite-customers-p.description:
Amplemarket wants to replace your SDR stack with one AI copilot. Here's what a handful of users, reviewers, and industry personalities had to say about that

I publish tool reviews on marketintelligencetools.com, and I just finished a long one on Amplemarket, which is a conflict when I'm the one asking for real opinions on it. I want to hear from people who've run real pipeline through it, especially anyone who came from Apollo, Outreach or Salesloft and can compare the switch directly.

Amplemarket bundles a 200-million-contact database, outreach across seven channels and an AI copilot called Duo into one contract. The Startup plan is $600 a month for two seats, billed annually, with no monthly option and no published free trial anywhere on the site. Fifteen thousand email credits and 480 phone credits per user come with it, plus two mailboxes.

Growth and Elite are both custom quotes, \u0026 neither publishes a number. Vendr's tracked-contract data puts the real median at $16,608 a year, ranging from $11,678 to $35,946. That's two to five times the advertised Startup rate, once a team needs the tiers Amplemarket won't price in public.

Has anyone here signed a Growth or Elite contract? I'd like to know if the number landed near that $16,608 median, or somewhere past the $35,946 high end Vendr has on record.

https://preview.redd.it/p0xzw646gxnh1.png?width=2400\u0026format=png\u0026auto=webp\u0026s=7d148659bd39779f86d253cc6ad019939fb54b6e

I pulled G2's own listing directly before posting this to make sure I get this right. Its aggregate is 4.6 out of 5 across 662 reviews as of 26 August 2026, with a 9.3-out-of-10 score for Quality of Support. Capterra's live listing matches on the headline number: 4.6 out of 5 across 7 reviews, 5.0 on customer service.

security-architects-and-ctos-orbital-ai-.headline: Security Architects \u0026 CTOs - Orbital AI Compute Claims
security-architects-and-ctos-orbital-ai-.description:
𝗔 𝗺𝘂𝗻𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗽𝗮𝗹 𝗱𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗰𝘁 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗱𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗮 𝘀𝗽𝗮𝗰𝗲-𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗵𝘂𝗯 𝗶𝘁 𝗱𝗶𝗱 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱. 𝗙𝗼𝗿 𝘀𝗲𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗖𝗧𝗢𝘀, an orbital satellite's headline power figure has moved twice in six weeks, and its most quoted performance claim belongs to a different product entirely.

On 31 August, Shanghai's Songjiang district opened a space-computing hub. It did not need to attract tenants. A state-backed satellite constellation operator was already resident there, alongside two satellite manufacturers and a precision-machinery research institute. The announcement formalised a cluster that already existed.

Four days later, an orbital AI compute satellite built by a launch provider and a chip maker was still working out what it actually is. Since the partnership's announcement on 24 August, its stated power draw has moved from 120 and 150 kilowatts, to 160 and 250, to 175 and 250, none of the earlier figures retracted. A widely repeated claim that it delivers twenty-five times the AI compute of a previous chip generation actually belongs to a different product the same chip maker announced in March, for six customers that do not include this launch partner.

Neither side's technology is shown to be superior here. What differs is what can be checked. Songjiang's tenants are verifiable entities that existed before this week's designation; the American partnership's own supporting detail has moved while I was watching it. Three questions do most of the work when a claim like this reaches your desk: where did the number first appear, has it changed since, and has it been attached to more than one product. Both this week's figures failed one of them.

An openly inspectable ground segment is available to any operator willing to build on it instead of around it. GNU Radio handles ground-station signal processing across the industry, and F Prime, the Jet Propulsion Laboratory's own open flight software framework, has flown on small-satellite missions since 2017. Vertical integration is a choice about who controls the stack, not a technical requirement of building one.

A New Zealand launch provider put a Japanese Earth-observation satellite into orbit this same week: real launch-site participation, but not tasking authority over what gets observed, and not the AI-enabled analysis that turns a radar return into something a board can act on. Owning the antenna and owning the analysis are separate capabilities.

Where has your organisation taken an orbital-compute claim at face value, only to find the number had moved, or belonged to a different product, once you went looking for the source?

This is one of seven weekly series in The Hamberger Report. Subscribe on LinkedIn and the next one arrives in your feed.

startup-engineers-retention-and-turnover.headline: Startup Engineers - Retention \u0026 Turnover Trends
startup-engineers-retention-and-turnover.description:
I've worked for two startups as an FTE and lasted 13 months and eight months respectively. 

Compare that to my job in 'legacy' newsrooms: 3 years, 5 years, 3.5 years. 

I don't think - as one former colleague sadonically suggested - that the problem is me (although I have - and do - describe myself as 'an outdoor cat'). 

Retention has been a problem at startups since the year dot. While the industry might have a reputation for free lunches, flashy off-sites, and equity packages, it also has one for engineers sleeping in tents and 9-9-6 work schedules. 

How big a problem is this in tech? And will it change? 

I'm working on a piece for the Financial Times. Get in touch with insights!
startup-engineers-retention-and-turnover.author: next-size-adjust
